I have recently started hitting the weights again. This time my goal is singular - lose weight. I know that weight-loss is 85% diet, so I'm focused on that.

I'm doing low carb because it has always been easier for me to portion than simply....well...portioning. The thing is, I have done paleo in the past and while I loved the results, the money was just too much. I can't afford to buy all that meat again. So I'm trying to do no complex carbs for 2/3 meals in the day. When I do eat them they are a side, I pile on the veggies, and I don't get seconds.

I just want to know if anyone else has had any luck with a similar diet. Most hardcore paleo (or god forbid - keto) dieters swear you need to completely eliminate grains and starches. I just don't want to do that again.

Paleo is a good beginner step, like a rehab for the sugary carb addicted. Once you're more advanced though, you start to realize how much better off your performance and sense of wellbeing are with a good amount of healthy carbs.

Personally I feel much better with plenty of dairy and whole wheat in my diet [I figure it's what my ancestors ate], I enjoy them, and I can get equally lean either way.

If you feel better with paleo-style clean eating, though, you might try paleo + rice.

Edit- almost forgot to mention the obvious: losing weight and getting lean is more about lowering calories while maintaining protein and strength levels than anything else. The bodybuilders of old did it on high-carb low-fat diets. Paleo isn't magical.
I totally agree. Paleo is the only diet I have ever gone on that actually helped me lose weight. My eating was so strict that when I got off, I binged on carbs. Stupid, I know.

I substitute grain with lentils. I take spirulina to get protein without having to eat tons of meat. Add turmeric as a spice to foods, since it helps burn fat. I am buff and lean, while being frugal at the same time.
Drink a protien shake before every meal. You'll save money on meat and feel more full.
The problem with such diets is that one inevitably goes off said diet, and the weight and bad habits come back. Portion control is the only path to consistent and long-term weight management.

I've had great results with minimal carbs, lots of veggies and the occasional chicken and fish for one meal only. My diet looks like this.

Organic protein shake for breakfast.
Big ass salad for lunch with a wheat roll and some peanut butter for lunch. A heaping pile of mixed veggies or another salad for dinner and a piece chicken, pork, or fish a couple times a week. If i don't have the roll for lunch, I'll have it with dinner.

With that plan and running 2 miles every other day I lost about 35lbs in 4 months. I still eat around that but I have days where I just eat more carbs, more meat, etc but I don't go crazy. I pretty much try to eat anything I want as long as the primary source of calories is veggies, fruit, nuts, and some meat, and minimal carbs. No alcohol, no pasta, no rice, no potatoes, no fries, no chips, limited sweets (dark chocolate covered nuts) and that's about it.

Right now I run or lift weights about 6 days a week, eat what I listed above, have some days where I eat some of things on the no-no list, enjoy some dark chocolate covered almonds in the eve to cure the sweet tooth, and I stay at a steady 188lbs.

Personally, I think marriage is outdated. But if you decide to get married, live together for a long time first. 2-3 years or more. Also, make sure this isn't "your first". If it is, get out there and live a little.

Marriage is a system that was intended to provide several benefits romantically, socially, and economically to the couple. As times have changed, so has the definition of marriage. What is important to remember is that while marrying for love is the primary motivation for most couples in today's society, marriage comes with as many consequences as benefits.

If you intend to become engaged to a person, that's ultimately a promise to become wed. Think very carefully about the implications. Is it a monogamous marriage or an open one? Is it economically or romantically motivated? Does this person know everything about you and your past, and vice versa?

The most successful marriages that I have seen in my personal life are marriages that took a long time to happen. Dating or "courting" is an important way to determine compatibility, and it can take more than a couple years to really see someone "let their guard down"

Engagement is the next logical step, but if you can see yourself marrying this person, it would be wise to make it an extended engagement to see how committed you are to actually tying the knot. This is more of a "little at a time" approach, as opposed to "jumping off the deep end".

Ultimately, talking about your ultimate goals with each other is the best way to determine the "length" question. Do you both want to have careers? Does she want to be a stay at home wife? Do you both want to be monogamous? Do either of you want kids? Sure, it may take away some of the romance but it's better than finding out your partner wants an open marriage and to pursue her career ten years and 2 kids into the marriage.

tl;dr: Take it nice and slow. Pressure to marry = Red flag. PRENUP. Communicate your ultimate goals with each other.
